theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why is a consultation done before a make-up service?
options: To sell the client as many retail products as you can
To find out what the client wants and check for contraindications
To agree the price only after the make-up is finished
To let the make-up artist try out any new look she likes on the client

questions.stem: What should be written on the client's record card for a make-up service?
options: Only her name, the date and the time she arrived at the salon
Her views on the other salons she has visited in the town
The price and the size of every product kept on the make-up trolley
Allergies, skin type, products used and the client's signature

questions.stem: A client, Shanice, wants make-up for a graduation at 3 p.m. in Spanish Town. Which question helps you most to design her look?
options: What colour is your outfit, and will the event be indoors or outdoors?
How much did you pay for the make-up you are wearing today?
Which of the other trainees working in the salon today do you like best?
Would you like to book a pedicure for some time next week?

questions.stem: Which eye condition stops an eye make-up service, so that the client is referred to a doctor?
options: Dark circles under both eyes
Hooded eyelids
Conjunctivitis (an eye infection)
Fine lines at the outer corners

questions.stem: A client has a cold sore on her top lip. What should you do?
options: Cover the cold sore with a thick concealer and carry on as normal
Apply the lipstick with your own finger so that no lip brush touches it
Do not do the service until it heals, and advise her to see a doctor
Squeeze the sore gently with a tissue, then draw lip liner around it

questions.stem: What is a contraindication?
options: A condition that means a service should not go ahead, or must be changed
A cleansing product that is used to take off make-up at the end of the day
A form the client signs to say that she has paid for the service
A colour that is chosen to match the client's outfit for the event

questions.stem: During the service, a client's eyelids become red, itchy and swollen after you apply eyeshadow. What should you do first?
options: Apply a thicker layer of eyeshadow on top to hide the redness
Finish the make-up quickly and then tell the client
Rub the eyelids firmly with a dry tissue to remove it
Stop, gently remove the product and apply a cool compress

questions.stem: How should lipstick be taken from the tube for a client?
options: Apply it straight from the tube onto the client's lips
Scrape a little onto a clean palette with a disposable spatula
Dip a lip brush into the tube and go back in after each stroke
Warm the tube in your hand and then dab it on with a finger

questions.stem: Why must a used disposable mascara wand never be put back into the mascara tube?
options: It can carry germs from the client's eye into the tube
It makes the mascara dry out and go lumpy too quickly
It wastes too much mascara on each of the client's eyes
It changes the colour of the mascara from black to brown

questions.stem: What is the difference between cleaning and disinfecting a make-up brush?
options: Cleaning kills every germ and spore; disinfecting only rinses the brush
There is no difference: both words mean washing the brush in water
Cleaning removes make-up and dirt; disinfecting then kills most germs
Disinfecting is done first, and cleaning is only needed once a week

questions.stem: Which method kills all micro-organisms, including spores, on metal tools such as tweezers?
options: Washing them in warm soapy water
Wiping them with a dry tissue
Keeping them in a UV cabinet
Sterilising them in an autoclave

questions.stem: How should a make-up pencil be prepared before it is used on each client?
options: Lick the tip to soften it before you use it
Sharpen it with a clean sharpener to give a new surface
Wipe it on the towel used for the last client
Warm it with a lighter so that it glides on

questions.stem: Which signs show that a client has oily skin?
options: Fine flaky patches, small pores and a tight feeling
Redness that comes and goes, and tiny broken veins
A shine on the skin, open pores and some blackheads
An even matt surface with no visible pores at all

questions.stem: Which foundation is usually the best choice for a client with dry skin?
options: A creamy, hydrating liquid foundation with a dewy finish
A heavy oil-free matte powder foundation
A thick layer of loose translucent powder
A clay-based mattifying gel with no oils

questions.stem: What is the best way to choose the shade of foundation for a client?
options: Test it on the back of her hand under the salon's yellow lights
Test a few shades on her jawline and check them in natural light
Pick a shade two tones lighter than her skin to brighten the face
Ask her which shade her friend uses and buy the same one for her

questions.stem: What is the 'undertone' of the skin?
options: The colour of the client's make-up from her last visit
The darkest patch of skin on the face, usually found under the chin
The thickness of the outer layer of the skin
The warm, cool or neutral tint below the surface colour

questions.stem: On a client with deep brown skin, why can a powder that is too pale be a problem?
options: It makes the foundation slide off within a few minutes
It makes the skin look oilier under the bright lights
It can leave a grey, ashy look that hides the skin's warmth
It turns orange as soon as it touches the skin

questions.stem: Which face shape is usually thought of as well balanced, so that little corrective work is needed?
options: Oval
Square
Round
Diamond

questions.stem: What does a highlighter (a shade lighter than the skin) do when it is placed on part of the face?
options: It makes that part look smaller and set further back
It brings that part forward so that it stands out more
It hides blemishes by turning them green in colour
It stops that part of the face from becoming oily

questions.stem: Where would you place a contour shade (darker than the skin) to make a round face look slimmer?
options: In the centre of the forehead and on the tip of the nose
Only on the eyelids, blending up to the brow bone
Across the apples of the cheeks in a round circle
Under the cheekbones and along the sides of the face

questions.stem: A client, Marsha, has a square face with a wide, strong jaw. Where should the contour shade go?
options: On the corners of the jaw, to soften the angles
In the centre of the chin, to make it look longer
Down the centre of the nose, from brow to tip
Across the whole forehead, from one side to the other

questions.stem: A client has close-set eyes (eyes that sit close together). Which eyeshadow method helps most?
options: Put the darkest shade on the inner corners near the nose
Use one dark shade evenly over the whole of each lid
Keep the inner corners light and add depth at the outer corners
Draw a thick line of eyeliner all the way round each eye to the inner corner

questions.stem: Which lip liner method makes thin lips look a little fuller?
options: Line well inside the natural lip line with a dark pencil
Line just on the outer edge of the natural lip line
Leave out lip liner and use only a dark matte lipstick
Line the lips with concealer to hide the natural edge

questions.stem: Which colour of corrector is used to cancel out redness on the skin, such as around the nose?
options: Purple
Pink
Yellow
Green

questions.stem: On deeper skin tones, which corrector colour usually cancels dark circles under the eyes?
options: Mint green
Bright white
Orange or peach
Pale blue or lilac

questions.stem: On the colour wheel, which colours are called 'complementary'?
options: Colours opposite each other, such as red and green
Colours next to each other, such as red and orange
Colours mixed with white, such as pink and lilac
Colours mixed with black, such as maroon and navy

questions.stem: Which are the three primary colours of pigment?
options: Green, orange and purple
Black, white and grey
Pink, brown and gold
Red, yellow and blue

questions.stem: What is the main job of a make-up primer?
options: To take off the old make-up before the new look is applied
To give a smooth base that helps make-up last
To add strong colour to the cheeks and lips
To clean the brushes between two clients

questions.stem: What is concealer mainly used for?
options: To set the foundation so that it does not move
To give shine to the centre of the lips
To cover blemishes, dark marks and dark circles
To thicken, lengthen and darken the upper and lower lashes

questions.stem: Why is a setting powder applied after foundation?
options: To set the base and reduce shine
To add a strong colour to the cheeks
To remove any extra cream products
To moisturise very dry skin

questions.stem: In Jamaica's hot and humid weather, which products help a bride's make-up last through an outdoor afternoon wedding?
options: A heavy face oil smoothed over the top of the foundation
An oil-control primer and a light setting spray
A thick rich night cream used as a base
Extra shimmer powder over the whole face

questions.stem: What does the open-jar symbol with '12M' printed on a make-up product mean?
options: The product contains twelve millilitres
The product must be stored for twelve months before use
The product is safe for children over twelve months old
Use the product within twelve months after opening it

questions.stem: When applying eyeshadow, where does the 'crease' colour usually go?
options: Only along the lower lash line, under the lashes
On the brow bone, under the brow
In the fold between the lid and brow bone
On the inner corner of the eye only

questions.stem: Where is a 'highlight' shade usually placed in eye make-up?
options: In the outer corner, blended into a 'V' shape
On the brow bone, just under the arch of the brow
Along the whole of the lower lash line, from corner to corner
Deep in the crease, to add depth to the eye

questions.stem: How should mascara be applied to the upper lashes?
options: From the roots to the tips, with a gentle side-to-side movement
From the tips to the roots, pressing hard on the lash line
Only on the tips, in one fast stroke straight upward
Onto the skin of the eyelid first, then brushed up onto the lashes

questions.stem: Which eyeshadow finish is usually best for a day look on mature skin with fine lines on the lids?
options: Heavy glitter
Frosted shimmer
Metallic foil
Matte or satin

questions.stem: When filling in brows with a pencil, which strokes look most natural?
options: One solid line drawn along the top edge of the brow
Large round dots of colour placed evenly along the middle of the brow
Short, light, hair-like strokes in the direction of growth
Heavy strokes drawn against the direction of the hair

questions.stem: Why is lip liner often applied before lipstick?
options: To moisturise the lips before the colour goes on
To shape the lips and stop the colour from bleeding
To remove dry skin from the lips before applying colour
To make the lipstick dry more quickly in hot weather

questions.stem: Which brush is best for applying loose powder lightly over the whole face?
options: A large soft powder brush
A small stiff angled brow brush
A thin fine eyeliner brush
A firm flat lip brush

questions.stem: How does evening make-up usually differ from day make-up?
options: It uses no foundation, concealer or powder at all on the face
It is lighter, with only clear lip gloss
It uses only one neutral colour all over
It is stronger, with deeper colours and more definition

questions.stem: Why is flash photography a concern when choosing products for a bride's make-up?
options: Flash makes all lipsticks look green in the photos
Flash causes waterproof mascara to run down the face
Some powders can show up white or pale in flash photos
Flash makes matte products look wet and oily on camera

questions.stem: What is a face chart used for in make-up design?
options: To plan and record the colours and placement for the look
To measure the client's face for a pair of glasses
To record the client's payment and the time of booking
To show the client a list of the salon's prices and opening hours

questions.stem: A client, Kerry-Ann, wants a look for a church wedding at 10 a.m. Which look suits the occasion best?
options: A heavy smoky eye with dark glitter and false lashes
Soft, natural colours with a light even base
Bright neon colours across the eyes and lips
Strong stage make-up with thick black liner

questions.stem: What is the best lighting for applying make-up?
options: Dim lighting in the room, so that the client can relax with eyes closed
Coloured lights, to show how the make-up will look at a party
A single bulb behind the client, so there are no shadows on you
Even, bright light on the face, as close to daylight as possible

questions.stem: Which advice should you give a client about removing her make-up at the end of the day?
options: Sleep in it overnight so the skin can soak up the products and oils
Rub it off with a dry towel to save time at night
Remove it with a suitable cleanser, then tone and moisturise
Wash it off with laundry soap and very hot water

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the small flat tool used to take a cream product out of its pot without touching it with your fingers?
Name the face shape that is about as wide as it is long, with full cheeks and a rounded chin.
What product is applied to the apples of the cheeks to add a natural flush of colour?
Name the skin type that is oily in the T-zone (forehead, nose and chin) but normal or dry on the cheeks.
What is the name of the small, painful, pus-filled lump on the edge of an eyelid, caused by an infection?
What one word is used for a germ that can cause disease, such as a harmful bacterium or virus?
On the colour wheel, what colour is made by mixing blue and yellow?
What is the name for using a shade darker than the skin to make part of the face look smaller or set back?
Which make-up product is applied to the lashes to darken, thicken and lengthen them?
What is the name of the loose, colourless powder often used to set foundation without adding colour?
What small brush, shaped like a mascara wand, is used to brush brow hairs into place?
What do we call a make-up look that uses soft, neutral colours so the client looks as if she is wearing very little make-up?
What must the client add to her record card to show that she agrees to the service?
Name the undertone of a skin that shows golden, yellow or peachy tints.
Many aerosol sprays and alcohol-based products catch fire easily. What one word describes such products?

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out a consultation with a new client before a make-up service. Say what you would ask, what you would look at and what you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: I sit the client in good light, greet her by name and explain that the consultation helps me plan a safe look for her. I ask about the occasion, the time of day, whether it is indoors or outdoors, the colour of her outfit and the kind of look she likes. I ask about allergies, sensitive skin, eye problems, contact lenses, medical conditions and any medicines or creams she uses. I look at her bare skin to find her skin type, skin tone and undertone, and any blemishes or dark marks. I check for contraindications such as eye infections, cold sores, cuts or rashes. We agree the look, the products and the price, and I sketch the plan on a face chart. I write her details, skin type, allergies, products and colours on the record card. She reads and signs it, I sign it too, and I keep it safe and private.
markingPoints: Asks about the occasion, time, setting, outfit and the look wanted
Asks about allergies, medical conditions, medicines and contact lenses
Checks skin type, tone and undertone, and looks for contraindications
Agrees the plan, products and price with the client (face chart)
Records the details on the record card, signed by the client and kept private

essays.stem: Explain the difference between cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising, and describe how you keep tools and products hygienic during a make-up service.
essays.modelAnswer: Cleaning removes make-up, oil and dirt with soap or brush cleanser and water. Disinfecting comes after cleaning: a salon disinfectant kills most germs on tools and hard surfaces if it is left on for the contact time the maker gives. Sterilising kills all micro-organisms, including spores, for example in an autoclave. Before each client I wash my hands, wipe the trolley with disinfectant and cover it with clean paper or a towel. I take creams and lipstick out with a clean spatula and put them on a palette, so the client never touches the main product. I sharpen pencils before each client. Mascara wands, sponges and applicators are disposable and used once only, and I never dip a used one back into a product. After the service, brushes are washed, disinfected as the maker allows and left to dry. Waste goes in a lined, lidded bin and towels go to the wash.
markingPoints: Correct difference between cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising
Washes hands and disinfects the workstation before each client
Takes products out with a spatula onto a palette; sharpens pencils
Uses disposable items once only and never double-dips
Cleans and disinfects brushes after use; deals with waste and towels correctly

essays.stem: Name conditions that would stop or change a make-up service, and explain what you would do if a client has a bad reaction during the service.
essays.modelAnswer: Some conditions stop the service, and the client is referred to a doctor: eye infections such as conjunctivitis or a stye, cold sores, impetigo, boils or any other skin infection. These can spread to other people and to other parts of her face. Other conditions mean I avoid the area or take extra care: cuts and grazes, bruising, swelling, recent scars, very sensitive skin, or a known allergy to a product. I do not try to name the illness. I explain kindly that the service cannot go ahead safely today and suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist. A bad reaction during or after the service is called a contra-action, for example redness, itching, swelling or watery, stinging eyes. If this happens I stop at once, remove the product gently with cool water or a mild cleanser, and apply a cool compress. I write what happened on the record card and advise her to see a doctor if it does not settle.
markingPoints: Names infections that stop the service (eye infection, cold sore, impetigo) and says why
Names conditions that restrict the service (cuts, bruising, allergy, sensitive skin)
Refers tactfully to a doctor or pharmacist without trying to diagnose
Explains a contra-action and stops and removes the product at once
Applies a cool compress, records the reaction and advises medical help if needed

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to prepare a client's skin before applying make-up, and say why good preparation matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the record card and make sure there are no contraindications. I protect the client's clothes with a gown and hold her hair back with a clean headband, then wash my hands. I remove any make-up she is wearing, starting with the eyes and lips, using a gentle remover on damp cotton pads. Then I cleanse the whole face with a cleanser that suits her skin type and remove it fully. I use toner on cotton to take off the last traces of cleanser and refresh the skin. Next I apply a moisturiser: a richer one for dry skin, or a light oil-free one for oily skin, and let it sink in. Last, I apply a primer for her skin, such as an oil-control primer on an oily T-zone. Good preparation gives a smooth, clean base, so the make-up goes on evenly and lasts longer, especially in hot, humid weather.
markingPoints: Protects the client (gown, headband) and washes hands
Removes old make-up, eyes and lips first
Cleanses and tones with products suited to the skin type
Moisturises with a product suited to the skin type
Applies a suitable primer and explains why preparation helps the make-up last

essays.stem: Explain how you would use highlight and contour to balance a round face and a long (oblong) face.
essays.modelAnswer: A highlight, lighter than the skin, brings an area forward. A contour, darker than the skin, makes an area look smaller or further back. Every shade must be blended well so that there are no hard lines. A round face is about as wide as it is long, with full cheeks. To make it look longer and slimmer, I place contour under the cheekbones, sloping down towards the corners of the mouth, and on the sides of the face near the temples and jaw. I place highlight down the centre of the face: the middle of the forehead, the bridge of the nose and the centre of the chin. A long face is much longer than it is wide. To make it look shorter, I place contour along the top of the forehead at the hairline and under the tip of the chin. I sweep blusher across the cheeks, more sideways than upward, and add highlight on the outer cheekbones to give width.
markingPoints: Highlight brings an area forward; contour sets it back
Round face: contour under the cheekbones and at the sides
Round face: highlight down the centre of the face
Long face: contour at the hairline and chin, blusher placed across the cheeks
Blends all shades so there are no hard lines

essays.stem: Jamaican clients have a wide range of skin tones. Explain how you would choose foundation, powder and colours to suit a client's skin tone and undertone.
essays.modelAnswer: Every client has a surface skin tone, from fair to very deep, and an undertone that is warm (golden or yellow), cool (pink or red) or neutral (a mix of both). The salon needs foundations in a wide range of shades. To choose one, I test two or three shades on the jawline and look at them in daylight. The right shade seems to disappear into the skin of the face and neck. Many deeper skin tones are not one even colour; they may be darker around the mouth, eyes or forehead. Then I may use two foundation shades, or a peach or orange corrector on the dark areas first. The powder must match the skin or be made for deep skin, because a pale powder leaves a grey, ashy look. For colour, warm undertones often suit golden, bronze and coral shades, and cool undertones suit pinks, plums and berry shades. Neutral undertones can wear most colours.
markingPoints: Explains skin tone and undertone (warm, cool, neutral)
Tests foundation on the jawline and checks it in natural light
Recognises uneven tone on deeper skin and uses two shades or a corrector
Avoids pale powder that leaves an ashy look
Chooses eye, cheek and lip colours to suit the undertone

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would apply eye make-up for an evening look.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the client's eyes are healthy and that there are no contraindications. I choose colours to suit her eyes, skin tone and outfit; for evening, deeper or shimmering shades can be used. I apply an eyeshadow base, or a thin layer of concealer, to the lids so the colour lasts and looks true. I sweep a medium shade over the lid. I add a deeper shade into the crease and the outer corner, and blend it upward and outward with a clean blending brush so there are no hard edges. I place a light highlight on the brow bone and in the inner corner. With the client looking down, I apply eyeliner close to the upper lash line and smudge or wing it to suit the look. I brush away any fallen powder from under the eye. I curl the lashes if needed and apply mascara from roots to tips with a disposable wand. Last, I check that both eyes match.
markingPoints: Checks the eyes are healthy and chooses colours for the client and the event
Uses a base or primer on the lid
Applies lid, crease and outer-corner shades, blended with no hard edges
Adds highlight and applies eyeliner close to the lash line safely
Applies mascara with a disposable wand and checks that both eyes are balanced

essays.stem: Compare day, evening and bridal make-up. Say how the products and colours change for each one, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: Day make-up is seen in natural daylight, which shows every detail, so it is light and natural: a sheer, even base, soft neutral eye colours, a little blusher and a natural lip colour. Evening make-up is seen in artificial or dim light, so it can be stronger: fuller coverage, deeper or shimmering eye colours, more defined eyeliner, false lashes if the client wants them, and a bolder lip. Bridal make-up must last many hours and look good both in person and in photographs. It is usually soft and flattering, chosen with the bride to suit her dress and wishes, using long-wearing and waterproof products and a well-set base. A trial is done some weeks before the wedding. For flash photos, avoid powders that show up white, and blend well so no harsh lines show. In Jamaica's heat, an oil-control primer, a setting spray and blotting papers help all three looks to last.
markingPoints: Day: light and natural to suit daylight
Evening: stronger colours and more definition for artificial light
Bridal: long-lasting, suits photographs and the dress
Mentions a trial before the wedding
Mentions products for heat or flash photography

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up a safe and hygienic make-up workstation before a client arrives.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose a clean area with bright, even light on the face, as close to daylight as possible. I set the chair at a height where I can work with a straight back, and where the client is comfortable with her head supported. I wipe the trolley with disinfectant and cover it with clean paper or a towel. I lay out clean brushes, sponges, spatulas, a palette, disposable wands, cotton pads, tissues, a clean headband and gown, and the products in the order I will use them. I put a lined, lidded bin close by. I check any lighted mirror or other electrical item for damaged cables and keep drinks and liquids away from it. I close the lids on products so they do not spill, and keep aerosols and alcohol-based products away from heat. I keep the floor clear of bags and cables so no one trips. Last, I have the record card and face chart ready.
markingPoints: Good, even lighting close to daylight
Correct chair height and posture for the therapist and the client
Disinfected trolley with clean tools and products laid out in order
Lined, lidded bin and disposable items ready
Controls electrical, spill, fire and trip hazards

essays.stem: Explain the aftercare and home-care advice you would give a client after a make-up service, and how you would recommend products to her honestly.
essays.modelAnswer: At the end I show the client the finished look in a mirror and check that she is happy. I advise her to blot shine with blotting papers instead of adding layers of powder, to avoid touching her face, and to touch up her lips after eating. At night she should remove all her make-up: eye make-up first with a gentle remover, then cleanse, tone and moisturise. She should never sleep in make-up, because it can block the pores and cause spots. She should not share mascara or eye pencils, and should replace mascara about every three months. If redness, itching or swelling appears later, she should remove the make-up and see a doctor. I may suggest a product I used, such as a primer or lipstick, but only if it meets her needs. I tell her the price clearly in J$ and never pressure her. I write the advice and any sales on her record card.
markingPoints: Checks the client is happy with the result
Gives advice on wearing and touching up the make-up
Gives the correct removal routine for the night
Gives hygiene advice (no sharing, replace mascara, act on irritation)
Recommends products honestly, gives the price and records the advice

practical1.title: Day make-up for a daytime event, planned on a face chart
practical1.brief: Work in pairs in the Centre's salon and take turns as make-up artist and client. In a group of five, one member works on a model who has agreed to take part. The assessor gives each member a daytime event, for example a graduation in Spanish Town or a job interview in New Kingston. Each member holds a consultation, completes and signs a record card with her client, checks for contraindications, and plans a day look on a face chart. She then prepares the skin and applies a day make-up: base, concealer, powder, brows, eyes, cheeks and lips. Each member also takes one job for the whole group: setting up the workstation, taking products out hygienically, taking the photos, or cleaning and disinfecting the tools at the end. Photograph each stage below. Take close-ups of the work area only (one cheek, one eye, the lips). Take a whole-face photo only if the client agrees in writing and the Centre allows it. Hand in once for the whole group, with the face charts and record cards.
materials: Make-up trolley or workstation with good light and a mirror
Cleansers, toners and moisturisers for different skin types
Primers, foundations in a wide range of shades (including deep shades), concealers and correctors
Setting powder, blushers, eyeshadows, eyeliners, brow pencils, mascara and lipsticks
Make-up brushes, disposable sponges, spatulas, palettes and disposable mascara wands
Cotton pads, tissues, headbands, gowns and clean towels
Brush cleaner, salon disinfectant and a lined, lidded bin
photos: The workstation set up, clean and laid out in order
Each member's face chart and record card (cover the client's private details)
Skin prepared and base applied: close-up of one cheek
Eye make-up and brows finished: close-up of one eye
Cheeks and lips finished: close-up of the lower face
Brushes and tools cleaned and the workstation cleared
checklist: Washed hands and disinfected the workstation before starting
Held a consultation, checked for contraindications and had the record card signed
Planned a look on the face chart that suits the event and the client
Prepared the skin correctly for its type
Matched the foundation on the jawline in good light
Took products out with a spatula and used disposable items once only
Blended the make-up evenly, with no hard lines, and balanced both sides
Gave aftercare advice and cleaned the tools and workstation
safety: Do not work on a client with an eye infection, cold sore, open cut or rash: tell the assessor
Never double-dip: use a new disposable applicator each time
If a product gets into the eye, rinse with plenty of clean cool water and tell the assessor
Stop and remove the product if the skin reddens, itches or swells
Keep aerosols and alcohol-based products away from heat, and keep cables tidy

practical2.title: Corrective and evening make-up for a special occasion
practical2.brief: The assessor gives each member a client card. It names an evening event (for example a dinner dance at a hotel in Montego Bay, or an awards night in Kingston), the colour of the outfit, and one feature to correct: a round face, a square jaw, close-set eyes, thin lips or dark circles. Work in pairs in the Centre's salon and take turns as make-up artist and client; in a group of five, one member works on a model who has agreed. Each member draws her corrective plan on a face chart, choosing a corrector, contour and highlight for her client's skin tone, and has the assessor check the plan. She then applies a full evening make-up with colour correction, contour and highlight, an evening eye and a defined lip. The group sets up one shared trolley, and each member cleans and disinfects her own tools at the end. Photograph each stage below, as close-ups of the work area only. materials: Make-up trolley or workstation with good light and a mirror
Colour correctors (green, peach or orange, lilac) and concealers
Foundations, contour and highlight shades in a wide range of skin tones
Eyeshadows in deeper and shimmer shades, eyeliners and mascara
Brushes, disposable sponges, spatulas, palettes and disposable wands
Face charts, client cards and record cards
Brush cleaner, salon disinfectant and a lined, lidded bin
photos: Each member's corrective plan on a face chart
Colour corrector applied: close-up of the area being corrected
Contour and highlight placed, before blending: close-up of one side of the face
Contour and highlight after blending: the same close-up
Finished evening eye: close-up of one eye
Tools cleaned and the trolley cleared
checklist: Chose the right corrector colour for the client's problem and skin tone
Placed contour and highlight correctly for the feature on the card
Blended all shades so that there are no hard lines
Applied an evening eye with depth, blended, and balanced on both eyes
Lined and filled the lips evenly in a colour that suits the outfit
Kept to hygienic practice throughout (spatula, palette, disposables)
Gave the client aftercare and removal advice
Cleaned and disinfected tools and left the area tidy
safety: Check for contraindications before starting and stop if the client reacts
Use only cosmetic glitter and products that are made for use near the eyes
Put any broken or used blade, for example from a pencil sharpener, in the sharps box
Keep aerosols away from heat and use setting spray with the client's eyes closed, in a ventilated area
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for every product
